questions.question: What is an API and why does software need them?
questions.answer: An API (Application Programming Interface) is a set of rules that allows one software application to communicate with another. Software needs APIs because applications are built in silos — your frontend doesn't know the internal workings of your backend, and shouldn't need to. APIs define a contract: 'send me a request in this format, and I'll respond with this format.' This decoupling lets frontend and backend teams work independently, lets companies expose their data to partners without giving database access, and lets different services communicate regardless of what language they're written in.

questions.question: What is a REST API and what makes it RESTful?
questions.answer: REST (Representational State Transfer) is an architectural style for APIs that uses standard HTTP methods and organizes data around resources identified by URLs. What makes it RESTful: (1) Resources are nouns in URLs — /orders, /users, not /getOrders or /createUser. (2) HTTP methods are the verbs — GET reads, POST creates, PUT updates, DELETE removes. (3) Stateless — each request contains all the information needed; the server doesn't remember previous requests. (4) Responses are representations of resources — typically JSON. REST is not a standard or protocol, it's a set of constraints that, when followed, produce consistent, predictable APIs.

questions.question: What is AWS API Gateway and what problem does it solve?
questions.answer: API Gateway is AWS's fully managed service for creating, publishing, securing, and monitoring APIs. The problem it solves: without it, you'd need to run your own web server (EC2) to receive HTTP requests, write routing code, build authentication, implement rate limiting, set up HTTPS, and build monitoring — all before writing a single line of business logic. API Gateway gives you all of this as a managed service. You define resources and methods (what URLs exist), set up integrations (where traffic goes), configure auth and throttling, and AWS handles all the infrastructure. You pay per request, not for idle capacity.

questions.question: Explain the difference between a resource and a method in API Gateway.
questions.answer: A resource is a URL path that represents an entity in your API — like /orders (a collection), /orders/{orderId} (a specific item), /users, or /payments. Resources form a tree structure starting from root /. A method is an HTTP verb attached to a resource that defines what action is allowed — GET /orders means 'retrieve orders', POST /orders means 'create an order'. The resource answers 'what are we working with?'; the method answers 'what are we doing to it?' Together they form the complete API surface: every combination of (resource path + HTTP method) is one API operation.

questions.question: What is Lambda Proxy Integration and why is it recommended?
questions.answer: Lambda Proxy Integration is an API Gateway setting where the full HTTP request is passed as a JSON event to Lambda — including httpMethod, path, headers, query parameters, pathParameters, and body. Lambda must return an object with statusCode, headers, and body. It's recommended because it's simple (no mapping templates needed), flexible (Lambda controls the complete response), and transparent (Lambda receives all request context including the calling user's IP, stage, authorizer results). Without Proxy Integration, you'd need to write VTL mapping templates to manually transform requests and responses, which adds complexity. Use Proxy Integration unless you have a specific need for request/response transformation at the API Gateway layer.

questions.question: What is a stage in API Gateway and why do you need multiple stages?
questions.answer: A stage is a named reference to a deployed snapshot of your API, representing an environment. Each stage gets its own invoke URL: /dev, /staging, /prod. You need multiple stages to safely manage the software development lifecycle. Dev stage: developers test new features here; connected to the latest Lambda code. Staging: pre-production testing; validated changes get promoted here. Prod: live users; only well-tested changes reach here. Stage variables add power — you can configure lambdaAlias=dev for the dev stage and lambdaAlias=prod for prod, pointing the same API definition to different Lambda versions. This gives you environment isolation, controlled rollout, and the ability to roll back by redeploying an older snapshot.

questions.question: What is CORS, why do you get CORS errors, and how do you fix them in API Gateway?
questions.answer: CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) is a browser security mechanism. The browser's Same-Origin Policy blocks JavaScript from calling APIs on different domains than the page's domain. For example, JavaScript at myshop.com cannot call execute-api.amazonaws.com without CORS headers. You get CORS errors when your API Gateway doesn't include the required Access-Control-Allow-Origin headers in its responses. Postman doesn't have this problem because it's not a browser — CORS is purely a browser enforcement. Fix: in API Gateway, select the resource → Actions → Enable CORS. This adds an OPTIONS method and the required headers. Then redeploy the API to the stage — without redeploying, the CORS change won't take effect. Common mistake: developers enable CORS but forget to redeploy.

questions.question: What is the difference between REST API and HTTP API in API Gateway?
questions.answer: REST API is the original, full-featured type — supports API keys, usage plans, response caching, WAF integration, request validation, response transformation, private endpoints, and more. HTTP API is a newer, simpler type that's approximately 70% cheaper but lacks those advanced features. HTTP API does support Lambda integrations and has built-in JWT authorizers. Rule of thumb: if you need API key management, usage plans, caching, WAF, or request validation — use REST API. If you're building a straightforward Lambda-backed API for your own application and just need cheap, fast HTTP routing — use HTTP API. The exam specifically tests this distinction.

questions.question: What is a Lambda execution role and what are the minimum permissions needed?
questions.answer: A Lambda execution role is an IAM role that Lambda assumes when running your function, granting it permissions to call other AWS services. Every Lambda function must have one. The minimum set of permissions needed for any Lambda function is the AWSLambdaBasicExecutionRole managed policy, which grants logs:CreateLogGroup, logs:CreateLogStream, and logs:PutLogEvents — the permissions needed to write execution logs to CloudWatch. Beyond that, add only what the function needs: dynamodb:PutItem for writing to DynamoDB, s3:GetObject for reading from S3, etc. Principle of least privilege — never attach AdministratorAccess to a Lambda function in production.

questions.question: Why must you deploy an API in API Gateway? What happens if you forget?
questions.answer: API Gateway separates the act of defining your API (creating resources and methods) from making it live (deploying to a stage). This is intentional — it lets you make many changes and test them internally before any external callers are affected. If you forget to deploy, clients continue calling the old version of your API. Changes to methods, integrations, authorizers, CORS settings, and throttle configurations are all invisible to callers until deployed. This is one of the most common mistakes: 'I updated my Lambda function name but the API is still calling the old one' — usually means the API wasn't redeployed after changing the integration.

questions.question: Tell me about a time you built a serverless API. What components did you use and what challenges did you face?
questions.answer: (Situation) I built an e-commerce orders API for a project using a fully serverless stack. (Task) The API needed to handle creating orders, retrieving order history, and returning 200/201/400 status codes correctly. (Action) I used API Gateway (REST API, Regional endpoint) with two resources — /orders supporting GET and POST — both connected to a Lambda function via Proxy Integration. The Lambda wrote to DynamoDB on POST and ran a scan on GET. I ran into three issues: First, CORS error when testing from the browser — fixed by enabling CORS on the resource and redeploying. Second, my changes weren't live — I forgot to redeploy after updating the Lambda integration. Third, Lambda couldn't write to DynamoDB — fixed by adding the DynamoDB write permission to the Lambda execution role. (Result) The API went live, handled concurrent requests cleanly, and cost less than $0.01 during testing.

questions.question: A client reports that your API returns 429 errors during peak traffic. What is happening and how do you address it?
questions.answer: (Situation) 429 Too Many Requests means API Gateway's throttle limits are being exceeded. (Task) Identify the limit being hit and reduce the impact. (Action) First, check the throttle limits: default account level is 10,000 RPS steady with 5,000 burst. Check CloudWatch metrics for API Gateway — specifically the 4xx error count and the Count metric by stage and method. If the issue is account-level: request a throttle limit increase via AWS Support. If the issue is specific to one expensive endpoint: add method-level throttling to restrict that endpoint without affecting the others. If the issue is read-heavy traffic: enable API Gateway caching on that method — responses are served from cache without hitting Lambda, massively reducing the effective load. (Result) Implemented caching with 60-second TTL on the product catalog endpoint, reducing Lambda invocations by 80% and eliminating the 429 errors.

questions.question: How would you implement different rate limits for three partner companies using your API?
questions.answer: (Situation) Three partners with different tiers — free (1K/day), standard (10K/day), premium (100K/day). (Task) Enforce per-partner limits without code changes. (Action) Create three API keys — one per partner. Create three usage plans matching each tier with the corresponding daily quota and rate/burst limits. Associate each API key with its usage plan. Mark the relevant API methods as requiring an API key (Method Request → API Key Required = true). Redeploy the API. Each partner includes their x-api-key header in every request. API Gateway automatically enforces the quota and throttle for each key. If a partner exceeds their limit, they get 429. (Result) Zero code changes to Lambda. Partners manage their own request budgets. Upgrading a partner is as simple as moving their key to a higher-tier usage plan.

questions.question: Explain the flow when a user logs in to your app and then calls a protected API endpoint.
questions.answer: (Situation) Mobile app using Cognito for user authentication. API Gateway protected with a Cognito Authorizer. (Task) Trace the complete auth + API call flow. (Action) Step 1: User opens the app and enters credentials. Step 2: App calls Cognito User Pool to authenticate. Cognito validates credentials and returns three tokens: ID token, access token, refresh token. Step 3: App stores the access token. Step 4: User taps 'View My Orders'. App sends GET /orders with header Authorization: Bearer [access-token]. Step 5: API Gateway's Cognito Authorizer intercepts the request, extracts the token, and validates it against the Cognito User Pool (signature, expiry, audience). Step 6: If valid, API Gateway allows the request through to the Orders Lambda. If invalid, API Gateway returns 401 Unauthorized immediately. Step 7: Lambda checks the user ID from the authorizer context, queries DynamoDB for that user's orders, returns JSON. (Result) Secure, managed user authentication with zero custom auth code.

questions.question: Your API works in Postman but gives a CORS error in the browser. Walk through your debugging process.
questions.answer: (Situation) CORS error in browser, works in Postman. This is immediately a CORS problem, not a Lambda problem. (Task) Identify the exact CORS misconfiguration and fix it. (Action) Step 1: Open browser DevTools → Network tab. Find the failing request. Look at the response headers — is Access-Control-Allow-Origin present? If not, CORS isn't configured. Step 2: Check API Gateway console — find the resource → confirm an OPTIONS method exists (created by CORS enable). Step 3: Check the OPTIONS method integration — does it return the correct headers? Step 4: Confirm the CORS configuration matches the frontend origin. * allows all origins, or specify the exact domain. Step 5: Critically — check the deployment. Is the current deployment including the CORS changes? Redeploy to the stage. Step 6: Test again in browser. (Result) 95% of the time the fix is either CORS not enabled on the resource OR CORS enabled but API not redeployed.

questions.question: How would you secure an API that will be called by both mobile app users and partner developers, each needing different access?
questions.answer: (Situation) Dual audience: end users (many, use JWT) and partner developers (few, need usage quotas). (Task) Single API, two auth paths. (Action) For end users: configure a Cognito Authorizer. Users log in via Cognito User Pool, receive JWT, include in Authorization header. API Gateway validates automatically. For partner developers: use API Keys + Usage Plans. Each partner gets a unique API key with a tailored usage plan (rate limits + daily quota). Partners include x-api-key header. At the method level: some methods require Cognito (user-specific resources like /orders/mine), others require an API key (bulk data endpoints, partner reporting). Some methods might require both. This layered approach ensures users can only access their own data, and partners are rate-limited to their contracted tier.

questions.question: What is the difference between a Lambda Authorizer and a Cognito Authorizer?
questions.answer: Lambda Authorizer: you write a Lambda function with any custom authentication logic. API Gateway calls it before the backend. It receives the incoming token (from header or query string), validates it however you choose (database lookup, custom signature verification, legacy auth system), and returns an IAM policy — allow or deny — plus optional context data passed to the backend Lambda. Use for custom token formats, proprietary auth, multi-tenant permission checks, or integration with non-Cognito identity systems. Cognito Authorizer: a managed integration with Amazon Cognito User Pools. You configure it by pointing to a User Pool, and API Gateway handles JWT validation automatically — no code needed. Use when your users are managed by Cognito and you want standard JWT-based authentication. Rule: custom or complex auth logic → Lambda Authorizer. Standard user auth with Cognito → Cognito Authorizer.

questions.question: How would you design an API that must only be accessible from within your corporate VPC, never from the internet?
questions.answer: (Situation) Internal API for microservices within a VPC — zero internet exposure. (Task) Configure API Gateway for VPC-only access. (Action) Step 1: Create the API as a Private API (not Regional or Edge-Optimized). This makes the API Gateway endpoint itself only reachable via a VPC Endpoint. Step 2: In the VPC, create a VPC Interface Endpoint for API Gateway (service: com.amazonaws.REGION.execute-api). This creates an ENI with a private IP in the VPC subnet. Step 3: Configure an API Gateway Resource Policy allowing access only from the VPC Endpoint ID (aws:SourceVpce condition). Step 4: Deploy and test from an EC2 inside the VPC — it should work. Test from the internet — it should fail with 403. (Result) API is completely invisible to the public internet. All traffic stays within the AWS network via PrivateLink.

questions.question: Describe the serverless architecture pattern and its cost advantages.
questions.answer: The serverless pattern (API Gateway + Lambda + DynamoDB) means no servers to provision, patch, or manage. Cost mechanics: API Gateway charges per million requests (roughly $3.50 for REST, $1 for HTTP). Lambda charges per invocation (first 1M free, then $0.0000002/request) plus duration (per millisecond, depends on memory). DynamoDB charges per read/write capacity unit on-demand. Compare to EC2: a t3.small runs 24/7 at roughly $15-20/month regardless of traffic. At low traffic (say, 100K requests/month) the serverless stack costs cents. At high traffic, it scales automatically — no capacity planning. The serverless stack also eliminates operational burden: no AMI patches, no OS updates, no Auto Scaling group management. The tradeoff: Lambda has a 15-minute max timeout (bad for long jobs), cold starts add latency for infrequently called functions, and debugging distributed serverless apps is harder than monolithic servers.

questions.question: How does API Gateway handle a sudden 10x traffic spike?
questions.answer: API Gateway itself scales horizontally and automatically — it's a managed service with no capacity limits on your part. However, two limits matter during spikes: Account-level throttle (default 10,000 RPS steady, 5,000 burst). If the spike exceeds this, requests get 429. Mitigation: request a limit increase, or implement caching to reduce effective load. Lambda concurrency limit (default 1,000 concurrent executions per region). If all 1,000 are used, new Lambda invocations are throttled. API Gateway returns 429. Mitigation: request concurrency limit increase, or use reserved concurrency per function to ensure critical functions always have capacity. For planned spikes (product launches, campaigns): pre-warm Lambda by sending test invocations, and pre-increase limits. For sudden unexpected spikes: 429 responses are returned and the client should retry with exponential backoff.

questions.question: What is idempotency and why does it matter for API design?
questions.answer: Idempotency means calling an operation multiple times produces the same result as calling it once. GET is idempotent — calling GET /orders 100 times always returns the same data and never changes state. DELETE /orders/42 is idempotent — deleting an already-deleted order still leaves the system in the same state. POST is NOT idempotent — calling POST /orders 3 times creates 3 orders. This matters for retry logic: if a client sends a POST and the network fails before receiving the response, should it retry? If yes, it might create duplicate orders. Solutions: use idempotency keys (client sends a unique request ID; server checks if it's already processed and returns the cached result instead of creating a duplicate). DynamoDB has built-in conditional writes for this. API Gateway can validate request bodies — use this to enforce required fields like a client-generated idempotency key.

questions.question: How would you implement API versioning in API Gateway?
questions.answer: Three common strategies: (1) URI versioning: include the version in the path — /v1/orders, /v2/orders. Each version is a separate resource tree. Cleanest for breaking changes. Clients explicitly choose their version. (2) Stage-based versioning: v1 = stage 'v1', v2 = stage 'v2'. Each stage has its own URL. Works well for major versions with long deprecation windows. (3) Header-based versioning: clients send Accept: application/vnd.myapi.v2+json. Requires a Lambda Authorizer or backend logic to route based on headers — more complex, not natively supported by API Gateway routing. Best practice: use URI versioning for public APIs (most explicit for consumers), maintain at least one previous version during deprecation periods, document version sunset dates clearly. API Gateway stage variables make it easy to point v1 and v2 stages at different Lambda aliases.

questions.question: Describe how you would use API Gateway with microservices — each service owned by a different team.
questions.answer: Architecture: one API Gateway per domain (not one per team), with each team owning their Lambda functions. The API Gateway has resources for each domain: /orders (owned by orders team), /users (users team), /payments (payments team). Each team's Lambda function is isolated — different IAM roles, different DynamoDB tables, different deployment pipelines. They deploy Lambda updates independently without touching API Gateway. Changes to API Gateway (new resources, methods) go through a shared API team or use infrastructure-as-code (AWS SAM or CDK) with a review process. This avoids the alternative (multiple API Gateways) which multiplies the number of URLs clients need to manage. Stage variables per environment ensure each team's dev Lambda connects to the dev stage, not prod. CloudWatch provides per-method metrics so each team can monitor their own endpoints.

questions.question: What are the security best practices for a production API Gateway?
questions.answer: (1) Always use HTTPS — API Gateway enforces this by default, never disable it. (2) Authentication: don't expose any method without an authorizer in production. Use Cognito for user-facing APIs, Lambda Authorizer for service-to-service. (3) WAF: associate AWS WAF with your REST API to block SQL injection, XSS, and IP-based attacks. (4) Throttling: configure method-level throttling for expensive operations even if account-level limits are high. (5) API Keys: use usage plans to prevent any single client from consuming all capacity. (6) Minimal permissions: Lambda execution roles should follow least privilege — only the specific DynamoDB table, specific S3 bucket, etc. (7) Resource policies: for private APIs, restrict access explicitly to known VPC endpoints. (8) Logging: enable CloudWatch access logging and execution logging on the stage. Set up alarms on 4xx and 5xx error rates. (9) Validate inputs: use request validators to reject malformed payloads before they reach Lambda.

questions.question: How would you use API Gateway caching effectively and what are its limitations?
questions.answer: Effective use: enable caching on GET endpoints that return data which changes infrequently — product catalog, configuration settings, public content. Set TTL based on how stale is acceptable (60 seconds for near-real-time, 3600 for static data). Use cache keys to vary cache by query parameter or header — e.g., cache /products?category=electronics separately from /products?category=books. Cost benefit: cached responses don't invoke Lambda, reducing Lambda costs. At high request volumes the cache cost is often less than Lambda invocation savings. Limitations: caching is REST API only (not HTTP API). Max TTL is 3,600 seconds. Cache size is configurable (0.5 GB to 237 GB) but costs money per hour. POST/PUT/DELETE requests bypass cache entirely — correct behavior since they modify data. Cache invalidation is manual (console or API call) — you can't invalidate by tags or patterns, only by stage or specific path. Cached responses can be stale — design your TTL conservatively for data that changes.
